body:
How the criteria work

The UNESCO World Heritage List uses 10 selection criteria. A nominated property must meet at least 1 criterion, demonstrate Outstanding Universal Value and satisfy the relevant requirements concerning authenticity, integrity, protection and management.

Criteria (i)–(vi) relate to cultural heritage. Criteria (vii)–(x) relate to natural heritage. The criteria help explain why a place has exceptional global significance; they are not simply labels for its age or appearance.

The 6 cultural criteria

CriterionCentral idea
(i)A masterpiece of human creative genius.
(ii)An important interchange of human values in architecture, technology, monumental arts, town planning or landscape design.
(iii)Exceptional testimony to a cultural tradition or a living or vanished civilisation.
(iv)An outstanding type of building, architectural or technological ensemble, or landscape illustrating a significant stage in human history.
(v)An outstanding traditional settlement or land- or sea-use showing a culture or interaction with the environment, especially where vulnerable to irreversible change.
(vi)A direct or tangible association with events, living traditions, ideas, beliefs or artistic and literary works of outstanding universal significance.

For criterion (vi), the Committee considers that it should preferably be used with other criteria. This wording is important: it expresses a strong preference rather than saying that criterion (vi) is never usable alone.

The 4 natural criteria

CriterionCentral idea
(vii)Exceptional natural beauty or outstanding natural phenomena.
(viii)Major stages of Earth's history, geological processes or significant landforms.
(ix)Important ongoing ecological and biological processes.
(x)Significant natural habitats for in-situ conservation of biodiversity, including threatened species of outstanding universal value.

Criterion (viii) is about geology and Earth's history, whereas criterion (ix) focuses on ecological and biological processes. Criterion (x) emphasises habitats important for conserving biodiversity.

How to distinguish similar cultural criteria

Criterion (ii) concerns an interchange of values that influenced cultural developments. Criterion (v) concerns an outstanding example of settlement or interaction with the environment. The Historic City of Ahmadabad is inscribed under both: the former recognises its architectural and cultural interchange, while the latter recognises its historic settlement pattern and pol neighbourhoods.

Criterion (iii) recognises exceptional testimony to a culture or civilisation. Criterion (iv) recognises an outstanding building type, ensemble or significant stage of history. Dholavira satisfies both because it provides evidence of Harappan civilisation and represents an outstanding form of Harappan town planning.

Criteria are necessary but not sufficient

A nominated property must also satisfy conditions intended to ensure that its value is credible and can survive:

  • Integrity: all properties must demonstrate sufficient wholeness and intactness.
  • Authenticity: properties proposed under cultural criteria (i)–(vi) must satisfy the applicable cultural authenticity requirement.
  • Protection and management: the property needs adequate long-term legal or other protective measures and an appropriate management system.

A mixed property must establish qualifying cultural and natural significance; having an attractive natural setting around a historic building is not enough by itself.

Prelims focus

  • There are 10 World Heritage selection criteria.
  • Criteria (i)–(vi) are cultural; (vii)–(x) are natural.
  • At least 1 criterion must be met, together with the other conditions for Outstanding Universal Value.
  • Criterion (vi) is preferably used with other criteria.
  • Integrity applies to all nominated properties; authenticity is specifically required for nominations under cultural criteria.
  • Trap: Satisfying a criterion without adequate integrity and management does not establish eligibility for inscription.

[Sources: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “The Criteria for Selection,” criteria (i)–(x), accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Operational Guidelines, WHC.26/01, 29 July 2026, paragraphs 77–119; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “Historic City of Ahmadabad,” Criteria (ii) and (v), accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “Dholavira: a Harappan City,” Criteria (iii) and (iv), accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Outstanding Universal Value rests on criteria, integrity, cultural authenticity, and protection and management; inscription requires a Committee decision.
pictures.caption: World Heritage inscription depends on meeting criteria and demonstrating lasting protection of Outstanding Universal Value.

title: The 10 UNESCO World Heritage Criteria: Cultural and Natural Heritage

body:
Nomination begins with the State Party

A local institution cannot directly place its own monument on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Under the Convention, the relevant State Party is responsible for preparing and submitting a nomination. In India, this requires coordination among the appropriate national, state and site-management institutions.

UNESCO's procedures change over time. The explanation below follows the Operational Guidelines dated 29 July 2026, document WHC.26/01, which are the applicable published guidelines at the content cutoff of 23 November 2026.

Stage 1: Tentative List

A Tentative List is a State Party's inventory of properties it may consider for future World Heritage nomination. It identifies potential candidates and briefly explains why they could possess Outstanding Universal Value.

Inclusion on the Tentative List is not World Heritage inscription. It does not establish that UNESCO has accepted a site's Outstanding Universal Value, nor does it mean that the property will necessarily be nominated.

Stage 2: Preliminary Assessment

Under the 2026 guidelines, a Preliminary Assessment is generally a mandatory desk-based process before a full nomination. It provides early expert advice about the potential for Outstanding Universal Value, integrity or authenticity, and management requirements. A State Party may still decide whether to proceed with a full nomination.

The Tentative List must be submitted at least 2 weeks before a Preliminary Assessment request. Information on the outcome of the Preliminary Assessment must be available at least 1 year before submission of the full nomination dossier.

There is a defined exception: qualifying site-specific Upstream Process advice may replace the Preliminary Assessment requirement when the nomination is submitted within the permitted 5-year period after receipt of the site-specific advice report, with that report annexed to the nomination. The Upstream Process is a voluntary early advisory mechanism.

Do not confuse the current rules with older summaries. In the 2026 guidelines, the key sequence is Tentative List, then Preliminary Assessment or a qualifying exception, then full nomination. The 1-year requirement relates to the Preliminary Assessment outcome before the dossier, not a blanket rule that every site must spend exactly 1 year on the Tentative List.

Stage 3: Prepare the nomination dossier

The nomination dossier is the formal evidence submitted to UNESCO. It must identify the property, explain its history and significance, justify the selected criteria, and present information needed to judge the proposed Outstanding Universal Value.

Important components include:

  • Property boundaries: accurate identification of the area that contains the significant heritage attributes.
  • Buffer zone, where necessary: an additional area around the property with protective restrictions supporting its conservation.
  • Comparative analysis: explanation of how the property compares with similar sites and why its value is exceptional.
  • Authenticity and integrity: evidence that the property meets the applicable conditions.
  • Protection and management: legal arrangements, responsible institutions, monitoring and arrangements for dealing with development or other threats.
  • Documentation: maps, photographs, records and supporting information.

Stage 4: Expert evaluation

The relevant UNESCO advisory bodies examine the nomination and provide assessments. ICOMOS evaluates cultural nominations, while IUCN evaluates natural nominations. They consider the criteria, comparative evidence, condition and conservation arrangements.

Stage 5: World Heritage Committee decision

The World Heritage Committee considers the nomination and advisory evaluation. It may:

  • Inscribe the property on the World Heritage List.
  • Refer the nomination for additional information.
  • Defer the nomination for more substantial revision or further assessment.
  • Decide not to inscribe the property.

For consideration at the Committee's session in the following year, a complete nomination dossier must ordinarily reach the World Heritage Centre by 1 February at 17:00 GMT, or by 17:00 GMT on the preceding Friday if 1 February falls on a weekend.

Inscription begins a continuing responsibility

A World Heritage property's management does not end at inscription. The responsible State Party must continue protecting the property's Outstanding Universal Value, managing development and visitors, and reporting on its state of conservation when required.

Prelims focus

  • India, as a State Party, submits World Heritage nominations.
  • Tentative List status is not the same as World Heritage inscription.
  • Under the 2026 guidelines, Preliminary Assessment is generally mandatory before a full nomination.
  • A Tentative List must precede a Preliminary Assessment request by at least 2 weeks.
  • The Preliminary Assessment outcome must be available at least 1 year before submission of the full dossier.
  • Trap: Advisory bodies evaluate nominations, but the World Heritage Committee makes inscription decisions.

[Source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Operational Guidelines for the Implementation of the World Heritage Convention, WHC.26/01, dated 29 July 2026, paragraphs 62–76, 120–160 and 168, including paragraphs 63, 65, 121, 122 and 128; accessed 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The 2026 nomination pathway separates possible candidates, assessed nominations and inscription, with timing rules and the qualifying Upstream exception.
pictures.caption: The 2026 procedure separates early listing, preliminary assessment, full evaluation and final inscription.

title: How a Site Enters the UNESCO World Heritage List: The 2026 Nomination Process

body:
Two UNESCO frameworks with different purposes

The 1972 World Heritage Convention concerns cultural and natural properties of Outstanding Universal Value. Historic cities, stepwells, archaeological sites and natural parks may fall within this framework.

The 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage focuses on living heritage: the practices, expressions, knowledge and skills that communities recognise and transmit across generations.

The two conventions are connected by their concern for heritage, but they operate through different criteria, processes and lists.

The 5 domains of intangible cultural heritage

Under the 2003 Convention, intangible heritage is commonly expressed through 5 broad domains:

  1. Oral traditions and expressions, including language as a vehicle of intangible heritage.
  2. Performing arts.
  3. Social practices, rituals and festive events.
  4. Knowledge and practices concerning nature and the universe.
  5. Traditional craftsmanship.

An intangible practice may involve instruments, clothing, utensils, buildings or other objects. Those objects have physical form, but the intangible element lies in the knowledge, cultural meaning and practice transmitted by people.

Safeguarding rather than freezing a tradition

The term safeguarding refers to measures that support the continued viability of intangible heritage. These can include identifying and documenting traditions, helping communities transmit skills, creating opportunities for practice and increasing public awareness.

Living heritage may evolve as communities adapt it to new circumstances. Safeguarding does not require every expression to remain identical to the way it was practised centuries ago. Participation by the communities that maintain the heritage is essential.

UNESCO's intangible heritage lists

  • Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity: increases awareness and visibility of living cultural heritage.
  • List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding: concerns elements whose continued viability requires urgent safeguarding measures.
  • Register of Good Safeguarding Practices: recognises programmes, projects or activities that demonstrate effective safeguarding approaches.

These mechanisms are not the same as the World Heritage List, the World Heritage Tentative Lists or the List of World Heritage in Danger.

Gujarat example: Garba

Garba of Gujarat was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2023. The recognised element is a living cultural practice sustained and transmitted by communities.

This recognition is different from the World Heritage inscription of Rani-ki-Vav, which concerns a physical stepwell property. Garba was not inscribed under any of the 10 World Heritage selection criteria, because those criteria belong to the separate 1972 Convention.

Why both forms matter

Built heritage and living traditions can support one another. A historic neighbourhood may preserve traditional buildings while its residents continue inherited practices. Conserving the buildings without considering the community may damage the living heritage associated with the place. Conversely, supporting traditions does not remove the need to protect important physical remains.

Prelims focus

  • World Heritage Convention: 1972; Intangible Cultural Heritage Convention: 2003.
  • The 2003 Convention recognises 5 broad domains of intangible heritage.
  • Garba of Gujarat entered UNESCO's Representative List in 2023.
  • The Representative List is separate from the World Heritage List.
  • Safeguarding intangible heritage includes continued transmission through communities.
  • Trap: Intangible heritage inscriptions are not selected using the 10 World Heritage criteria.

[Sources: UNESCO, Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, 2003, Articles 2 and 16–18, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage, “Garba of Gujarat,” Nomination 01962 and Decision 18.COM 8.b.32, accessed 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, “The Criteria for Selection,” accessed 23 November 2026; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Chapter 1, “Crafts Heritage,” printed pp. 9–14.]

pictures.alt: Rani-ki-Vav and Garba are both heritage, recognised under different UNESCO conventions and lists, with different selection and safeguarding approaches.
pictures.caption: A physical heritage property and a living cultural tradition can both be significant without belonging to the same UNESCO list.
